content: Chromium is a chemical element with the symbol Cr and atomic number 24. It is a steel-gray, lustrous, and hard metal that is capable of taking a high polish. It has a high melting point and is both odorless and tasteless. Additionally, it is malleable, making it suitable for various applications. In 1761, Johann Gottlob Lehmann discovered an orange-red mineral in the Ural Mountains, which he named Siberian red lead. Although initially misidentified as a lead compound containing selenium and iron, it was later determined to be lead chromate (PbCrO4), now known as the mineral crocoite. In 1770, Peter Simon Pallas also studied this mineral and noted its utility as a pigment in paints. The use of crocoite as a pigment quickly gained popularity, particularly for producing a bright yellow color. In 1797, Louis Nicolas Vauquelin received samples of crocoite ore and successfully produced chromium oxide (CrO3) by reacting the ore with hydrochloric acid. By 1798, Vauquelin had isolated metallic chromium by heating the oxide in a charcoal oven. He also detected traces of chromium in gemstones such as rubies and emeralds. During the 19th century, chromium was primarily used in paints and tanning salts. Today, approximately 85% of chromium is used in metal alloys, with the remainder utilized in the chemical, refractory, and foundry industries. The name chromium is derived from the Greek word chrôma, meaning color, due to the vibrant hues of its compounds. Chromium is primarily mined as chromite (FeCr2O4) ore. South Africa is the largest producer, accounting for about two-fifths of global production. Other significant producers include Kazakhstan, India, Russia, and Turkey. Untapped chromite deposits are abundant, particularly in Kazakhstan and southern Africa. In 2000, approximately 15 million tons of chromite ore were mined, yielding around 4 million tons of ferrochrome, valued at approximately $2.5 billion USD. Although native chromium deposits are rare, some have been discovered, such as in the Udachnaya Mine in Russia, where the reducing environment also facilitates diamond formation. Commercially, chromium is extracted by heating chromite ore in the presence of aluminum or silicon. Chromium belongs to the transition metals and is part of group 6 on the periodic table. Its electronic configuration is 4s1 3d5, which reflects the stability of its high-spin configuration. Chromium exhibits a variety of oxidation states, with +2, +3, and +6 being the most common. The +3 state is the most stable, while +6 compounds are strong oxidizing agents. Chromium forms a protective oxide layer when exposed to oxygen, which prevents further oxidation. This passivation property is enhanced when combined with elements like nickel or iron, forming a dense spinel structure that inhibits oxygen diffusion. Chromium is often plated over a nickel layer, sometimes with an additional copper layer beneath. Unlike many metals, chromium does not suffer from hydrogen embrittlement but is susceptible to nitrogen embrittlement, which has hindered the development of straight chromium alloys. Potassium dichromate is a potent oxidizing agent commonly used to clean laboratory glassware of organic residues. It is typically used as a saturated solution in concentrated sulfuric acid. Sodium dichromate is sometimes preferred due to its higher solubility. Chromium(III) oxide (Cr2O3), also known as chrome green, is used in enamel painting and glass staining. Chrome yellow (PbCrO4) is a vivid yellow pigment historically used by painters. Chromic acid (H2CrO4) and dichromic acid are not naturally occurring but exist in various compounds. Chromium trioxide (CrO3), the anhydride of chromic acid, is sold industrially under the name chromic acid. Chromium is unique in its ability to form quintuple covalent bonds. A compound containing a quintuple bond between two chromium atoms was synthesized using a bulky monodentate ligand, which prevented further coordination. This bond was confirmed via X-ray diffraction, with a bond length of 183.51 pm. Chromium remains the only element for which quintuple bonds have been observed. Chromium has numerous applications. In metallurgy, it is used to enhance corrosion resistance and provide a shiny finish, such as in stainless steel and chrome plating. It is also used in anodized aluminum, which can produce a ruby-like surface. Chromium compounds are used as pigments in dyes and paints, with chromium(III) oxide serving as a green polish and chromium salts imparting an emerald green color to glass. Chromium is responsible for the red color of rubies and is used in synthetic ruby production. It also produces a brilliant yellow pigment for painting. Chromium compounds are used as catalysts, in leather tanning, and in the production of magnetic tape. Potassium dichromate is employed as a reagent for cleaning glassware and as a mordant for fabric dyes. Chromium(IV) oxide (CrO2) is used in magnetic tape manufacturing due to its superior coercivity compared to iron oxide. Chromium is also used in well-drilling muds, as a dietary supplement, and as a gasoline additive. Chromium boride (CrB) serves as a high-temperature electrical conductor, while chromium(III) sulfate is used as a green pigment in paints and ceramics. Chromium(VI) is used in the preparation of gravure printing cylinders to enhance their durability. Biologically, trivalent chromium (Cr(III)) is an essential trace element required for sugar metabolism in humans. Its deficiency can lead to a condition known as chromium deficiency. In contrast, hexavalent chromium (Cr(VI)) is highly toxic and mutagenic when inhaled. While Cr(VI) has not been definitively established as a carcinogen when ingested, it is known to cause allergic contact dermatitis. Chromium picolinate, a popular dietary supplement, has been shown to cause chromosomal damage in laboratory studies. The recommended daily intake of chromium for adults in the United States has been revised to 35 µg for men and 25 µg for women. Chromium has three naturally occurring stable isotopes: 52Cr, 53Cr, and 54Cr, with 52Cr being the most abundant. Nineteen radioisotopes have been identified, with 50Cr and 51Cr being the most stable. Chromium isotopes are used in isotope geology to study the early history of the solar system. Variations in 53Cr/52Cr and Mn/Cr ratios in meteorites provide evidence of nucleosynthetic processes preceding the formation of the solar system. Chromium metal and chromium(III) compounds are generally not considered hazardous to health. However, hexavalent chromium compounds are highly toxic if ingested or inhaled. The World Health Organization recommends a maximum allowable concentration of 0.05 mg/L of Cr(VI) in drinking water. Hexavalent chromium is also restricted under the European Restriction of Hazardous Substances Directive. Due to its historical use in dyes, paints, and leather tanning, chromium contamination is often found in soil and groundwater at abandoned industrial sites, necessitating environmental remediation. Primer paints containing Cr(VI) are still widely used in aerospace and automotive refinishing.
